text: Every company has an AI assistant now. And they all test it the same way. Save some real conversations, check the answers by hand, run them before every release. Green means ship.

Here's mine. A support bot for a hardware shop. A customer asks to cancel an order. The database says it was already delivered. The bot says: it's been delivered, and it can't be cancelled, because it's out for delivery. It can't be both. It just said both.
So I wrote tests. Fifty real conversations, every answer checked by hand. Like unit tests, but for a chatbot. They pass. Every release.
Then the business changed. The shop started renting out tools. Deposits, late fees, damage charges. By week eight, half of everything people asked was rentals.
My tests had zero rental questions. I wrote them before rentals existed. And they still passed. Every single time.
So I built something to ask what my tests couldn't. First. How much of what people ask today do my tests even look like? Week one, seventy seven percent. Week eight, thirty.
Second. If the bot got worse at rentals tomorrow, would my tests notice? So it breaks the bot on purpose, four hundred times, and counts how often the tests go red. One percent.
Pass. Fail. And a third answer nobody gives you. Blind. Not you're fine. I can't tell, and here's the number that says why.

It checks the grader too. Because an AI is grading these answers, and that costs real money. Could something cheaper do it? Keywords, word counts, a bag of features. It tries all of them against the judge. Nothing comes close. So the expensive one is earning its keep, and now I can prove it.
Then it fixes it. It goes back through your real traffic and pulls out the conversations your tests can't see. Real customers. Real questions. It never invented one.
They land in a review queue. You click right, or wrong. A person, not the AI. Let the AI grade its own homework and you've proved nothing.
Same traffic. Same bug. Same everything. How much my tests look like today's questions: thirty percent, up to sixty. Would they catch that rentals bug? One percent, up to forty three.
Everyone knows tests go stale. Nobody has a number for how stale yours are right now. That's the whole thing. Runs on your machine. Costs nothing.
